subject: physiology
title: Oxygen and carbon dioxide transport

steps.tx: Oxygen travels in blood in two ways. Almost all of it, roughly 97 to 99 percent, rides on **haemoglobin**. The rest is dissolved in plasma. Each haemoglobin molecule has four haem groups, so it can carry four oxygen molecules. Dissolved oxygen follows Henry's law, so its amount rises in direct proportion to its partial pressure. Because dissolved oxygen is a small fraction, haemoglobin governs most of what the tissues receive.

steps.tx: The **oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve** is sigmoid because haemoglobin shows **positive cooperativity**: each bound oxygen makes further binding easier. Haemoglobin shifts between a low affinity **T state** and a high affinity **R state**. **Myoglobin** has a single binding site, so its curve is a rectangular hyperbola with no cooperativity. Its higher affinity lets it accept oxygen from haemoglobin in muscle and store it to support sustained contraction.

left.title: Haemoglobin
points: Shifts between T and R states

steps.tx: Shifts of the curve change how readily haemoglobin releases oxygen. A **right shift** lowers affinity and favours unloading. It follows a rise in CO2, a fall in pH, a rise in temperature, and more **2,3-BPG**. This is the Bohr effect. A left shift does the opposite and is seen with fetal haemoglobin, carbon monoxide, alkalosis and hypothermia. Stored blood loses 2,3-BPG, so it shifts left. Chronic hypoxia raises 2,3-BPG and shifts the curve right.

rows: Rise in CO2 or fall in pH

steps.tx: Carbon dioxide is carried mainly as **bicarbonate**, about 70 percent. Carbamino compounds on haemoglobin account for about 23 percent, and dissolved CO2 about 7 percent. In the tissues, CO2 enters red cells and forms bicarbonate. Bicarbonate leaves the cell in exchange for chloride through band 3, which is the **chloride shift**. Venous haematocrit is therefore slightly higher than arterial. The **Haldane effect** describes how oxygenated haemoglobin releases more CO2 in the lungs.

steps.tx: **Carbon monoxide** binds haemoglobin with an affinity more than 200 times that of oxygen. It cuts oxygen-carrying capacity and also shifts the curve left, so tissues get less oxygen. Carboxyhaemoglobin is cherry red, which can mask cyanosis. Treatment is high-flow oxygen, and in severe cases hyperbaric oxygen. Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output, haemoglobin level, dissolved oxygen and the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. Indian and US texts agree on these principles.

vis.alt: Oxygen haemoglobin dissociation curves: normal sigmoid curve with P50 of 26.6 mmHg, a right shifted curve with easier oxygen release, a left shifted curve with tighter binding, and a carbon monoxide curve that is both left shifted and lowered; arterial and venous points marked.
vis.caption: Right shift (acid, CO2, heat, 2,3-BPG) unloads oxygen; left shift and carbon monoxide trap it, so tissues are starved even at normal PaO2.
